title: Reach End of Array With Max Score
statement:
You start on index `0` of the integer array `nums` and must finish on its last index, `nums.length - 1`. Every move is a forward jump: from index `i` you may land on any index `j` with `j > i`, and that jump earns `(j - i) * nums[i]` points.

Return the largest total of points that any sequence of jumps from index `0` to the last index can earn. If `nums` has only one element you are already at the end, so the total is `0`.
notes:
## Intuition

A jump from `i` to `j` pays `nums[i]` for each of the `j - i` steps it covers. So think of the value of the index you stand on as your **rate**: every single step forward earns the rate of the index you last jumped from. The step from position `k` to `k + 1` is always paid by some index at or before `k`, so it can never earn more than the largest value among `nums[0..k]`. That bound is reachable: keep walking past values that are no larger than your rate, and land on the first strictly larger value you meet, which raises your rate as early as possible. Trying every pair `(i, j)` in a DP also works but costs O(n²).

## Approach

1. Let `last` be the final index, `score = 0`, and `from = 0` (the index you stand on).
2. Scan the possible landing spots `to` from `1` to `last`.
3. Jump when `nums[to] > nums[from]` (a better rate) or when `to === last` (you must finish there).
4. A jump adds `(to - from) * nums[from]` to `score` and moves `from` to `to`.
5. Return `score`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [1, 3, 1, 5]`, so `last = 3`. Standing on index 0 (rate 1), `to = 1` holds 3 > 1: jump, `score = 1 * 1 = 1`, `from = 1`. At `to = 2` the value 1 is not above 3, so keep going. `to = 3` is the last index: `score += (3 - 1) * 3 = 6`, giving `7`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one pass over the indices.
- Space: O(1): a few counters.

## Pitfalls

- Jumping straight to the largest value ahead is wrong: the steps before it are still paid at your current, lower rate. In `[1, 2, 3]` that gives 2 instead of 3.
- Do not forget the final jump onto `last`; without the `to === last` test the distance after the last record is never paid.
- The last element's own value never earns anything, since nothing jumps from it.
- Totals reach about 10^5 · 10^5 = 10^10, beyond a 32-bit int, so use `long` in Java and C.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `last` | the index the trip must end on |
| `score` | points earned by the jumps made so far |
| `from` | the index you stand on; `nums[from]` is your rate per step |
| `to` | the candidate index to land on next |

narration.2: The trip has to end on the last index.
narration.3: No jumps yet, so no points.
narration.4: You start on index 0; its value is the rate each step earns.
narration.6: Consider every later index, left to right, as a landing spot.
narration.7: Jump when this index offers a strictly higher rate, or when it is the end and you must land.
narration.8: The jump covers to - from steps, each paid at the rate nums[from].
narration.9: Stand on the new index; its value is now your rate.
narration.12: The last index is reached; return the total score.
